results.summary: This design implements a binary-to-decimal decoder that converts an 8-bit binary value into signals for a 7-segment display. It uses simple AND and OR gates to produce the segment outputs, but the provided documentation only shows partial truth tables for a few inputs and outputs, making the full mapping unclear. The project is intended to drive a 7-segment display directly, with no external hardware required. Testing is described through truth tables, but the incomplete documentation limits verification of the complete design.

This project implements a tapped delay line using a chain of inverters and flip-flops, with eight tap outputs and a multiplexer to select which tap to observe. It is designed to measure the propagation delay between start and stop signals, serving as a characterization test for future projects. External hardware such as a signal generator and possibly an FPGA is suggested for testing. The design's main purpose is to evaluate timing characteristics, and no silicon results are provided.

This design is a 4-bit Johnson counter that generates four offset square waves at one-quarter of the input clock frequency. It is built from four D flip-flops connected in a ring with the inverted output of the last stage fed back to the first. The outputs can be verified with a logic analyzer to observe the expected repeating pattern. No external hardware is required, and the design is a straightforward sequential logic example.

This project counts from 0 to 7 and displays the digit on a 7-segment LCD, incrementing every second. It converts a 3-bit binary-coded decimal to the seven segment outputs using truth tables, sum-of-products, Boolean simplification, and Karnaugh mapping. The design is controlled by a clock switch and a reset button to start from zero. No external hardware is needed, and it appears to be an educational exercise in combinational logic design.

This design outputs both the AND and NAND of two input signals, providing two separate outputs from the same inputs. It is a simple combinational logic block with no clock or sequential elements. Testing involves applying signals to the two inputs and observing the corresponding outputs. No external hardware is required, and the project serves as a basic demonstration of logic gates.

This design is a 2-bit to 7-segment display driver that converts a 2-bit binary input (0-3) into the corresponding segment outputs for a 7-segment display. The outputs map to segments a through g and the decimal point. It can be driven by any external signal source, and no specific external hardware is required. The project is described as a first Tiny Tapeout attempt and provides a simple introduction to display decoding.

This project contains an AND gate that combines two inputs and drives an LED output. The documentation is minimal, with only a single input pin listed and no clear explanation of the second input or the testing procedure. It appears to be a first attempt at using the Wokwi design environment. No external hardware is mentioned, and the design's functionality is not fully described.

This design is a rhythm sequencer and randomizer that uses an 8-stage ring counter or LFSR to generate looping or pseudo-random patterns on eight outputs. It is controlled by three switches: one selects between looper and randomizer modes, another toggles to create a new loop, and a third clears the pattern or allows input of a custom rhythm. The outputs can drive external hardware via the Tiny Tapeout GPIO pins. Testing involves a specific sequence of switch operations to clear, start, and randomize the pattern.

This project implements a 4-bit adder that takes two 4-bit numbers as inputs and produces their sum. The documentation is sparse, with no details on the output pins or the exact behavior, and the testing suggestion is to use a truth table. No external hardware is specified, and the description is tentative, indicating it is a work in progress. The design appears to be a basic arithmetic exercise.

This project is a placeholder with no functional description, only listing two inputs (A and B) and two outputs (S and C), which suggests a half-adder, but the documentation is entirely template text. No explanation of how it works or how to test it is provided. No external hardware is mentioned. The design is essentially undocumented and cannot be evaluated.
